items.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing to use his return atop a powerful Senate committee to push for sweeping changes to the nation's healthcare system, setting up an early test of how far Democrats are willing to go in embracing progressive priorities.

items.title: ‘Neighbourhood support teams’ to pave way for national care service, Cooper announces
items.summary:
Health secretary said programme would help about 566,000 vulnerable people in England by April

More than half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will be offered help from joint NHS and social care teams that will pave the way for the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced.

Elderly people, care home residents, those with dementia and people near the end of their lives will receive assistance from the new programme.

items.summary:
In a statement celebrating the historic drop in drug deaths, the White House pointed to successes since President Trump took office. In fact, the biggest progress happened under the Biden administration.

items.t: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit

items.title: Bacterial toxin produced by E coli leading suspect in rise in bowel cancer among under-50s
items.summary:
Scientists tell Commons exposure to colibactin in early life is potential driver of early-onset colorectal cancer

Exposure to a bacterial toxin in early life has emerged as a leading suspect in the rise of bowel cancer among those under 50, MPs have heard.

Cases of early-onset bowel cancer have doubled in many countries in the past two decades, and while rising obesity and a fall in physical activity are contributors, researchers believe other factors must also be involved.

Continue reading...
items.t: Bacterial toxin produced by E coli leading suspect in rise in bowel cancer among under-50s

items.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
items.summary:
Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon

Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place (BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November).

The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies.

Continue reading...
items.t: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter

items.title: Why Palantir’s health tech is not the right fit for the NHS | Letter
items.summary:
The US firm’s health data system is based on an insurance model of healthcare, not the patient-centred universal service we have in Britain, says Prof Caroline Mitchell

The news that NHS England may have overstated the benefits of Palantir for improving efficiency will surprise few frontline clinicians (NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools, 12 November)

Too often, global digital policy assumes that software designed for the fragmented, insurance-based US healthcare system can simply be adapted to a universal public service elsewhere. A legitimate concern is that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature in the NHS context, having been developed primarily for a very different US healthcare system.

Continue reading...
items.t: Why Palantir’s health tech is not the right fit for the NHS | Letter

items.title: Anti-vaccine group once led by RFK Jr back on Facebook and Instagram after being banned
items.summary:
Children’s Health Defense was removed from Facebook and Instagram in 2022. Meta declined to comment on why it allowed the group back

An anti-vaccine group led for years by Robert F Kennedy Jr has been allowed back on Facebook and Instagram, four years after Meta removed the group for repeatedly violating its misinformation policies.

A review by the Guardian found that Children’s Health Defense (CHD) has reopened or opened six accounts on Facebook and Instagram from May through September this year. The group is using its accounts to share false and misleading information about topics including vaccines and deadly measles outbreaks at a time when measles has come roaring back. Health officials have reported 10 measles-associated deaths in the United States this year, and the country this week lost its measles elimination status in an official recognition that it is again endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.

Continue reading...
items.t: Anti-vaccine group once led by RFK Jr back on Facebook and Instagram after being banned

items.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
items.summary:
A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything

The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.”

It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”.

Continue reading...
items.t: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck

items.title: Cancer patients at NHS trust harmed by years of unnecessary chemotherapy, report finds
items.summary:
Trust apologises after findings on treatment of 20 brain tumour patients under oncologist who retired in 2023

Cancer patients were severely harmed after being given years of unnecessary chemotherapy treatment by an NHS trust, a report has found.

Some people were misdiagnosed and given inappropriate courses of treatment, while others were incorrectly told that if they stopped chemotherapy they would die, according to a Royal College of Physicians (RCP) report.

Continue reading...
items.t: Cancer patients at NHS trust harmed by years of unnecessary chemotherapy, report finds

items.title: The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe
items.summary: After dismantling the United States Agency for International Development, the Trump administration is restarting foreign aid. In Zambia and Zimbabwe, there are different approaches but similar worries.
items.t: The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe

items.title: Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial
items.summary:
Exclusive: Jury was never told that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was barred from practising over concerns for patients’ safety

A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial over fears he posed a risk to their safety.

Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that the British nurse had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told.

Continue reading...
items.t: Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial

items.title: A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that a rare, potentially life-threatening inflammatory disorder is driven by malfunctioning immune cells, overturning three decades of scientific understanding. The breakthrough points to a promising new treatment using existing medications, with one severely affected infant already showing substantial improvement.
items.t: A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

items.title: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
items.summary: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people.
items.t: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

items.title: ‘I’m heartbroken’: experts dismayed as US loses long-held measles elimination status
items.summary:
Public health leaders condemn ‘significant damage’ by Trump administration as calls grow for RFK Jr to resign

Doctors and public health leaders expressed grief and alarm at the loss of US measles-free status, a hard-won public health victory that once made the US a leader in infectious disease elimination.

Measles was declared resurgent in the United States, Bolivia and Mexico by the Pan American Health Organization (Paho) on Tuesday, meaning the virus has spread continuously for 12 months.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘I’m heartbroken’: experts dismayed as US loses long-held measles elimination status

items.title: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.
items.t: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

items.title: Yvette Cooper announces new health support for most vulnerable people in England
items.summary:
Health secretary says 500,000 will benefit initially from ‘downpayment’ on PM’s national care service pledge

  • UK politics live – latest updates

Half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will get proactive help with their health needs from new teams that will act as a “downpayment” on the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced.

Elderly people, care home residents, those with dementia and people near the end of their lives will receive help from new joint teams of NHS and social care staff. Initially about 500,000 people by next April will benefit from new joined-up support teams providing personalised care.

Continue reading...
items.t: Yvette Cooper announces new health support for most vulnerable people in England

items.title: Get vaccinated, don’t vape – and moisturise liberally! 10 doctors on how to avoid and treat winter ailments
items.summary:
The nights are drawing in, the temperature is dropping, festive overindulgence is on the horizon and it’s easy to get run down. Here’s some expert advice to help you safely through the season

Winter can be a challenging time, with bad weather, dark evenings, horrible bugs circulating, plus plenty of opportunities for overindulging. How can we avoid getting run down? Doctors share their tips for surviving the season, from saunas to screen blockers, light boxes to apples.

items.title: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records
items.summary:
Campaign groups and regulators say data breaches are distressing for patients and families and erode trust in the health service

The NHS in England has recorded more than 3,000 incidents of staff inappropriately snooping on patients’ medical records in the last five years.

Patient campaign groups and regulators said the figures were “deeply concerning” and distressing for patients and families, and eroded trust in the health service. A lack of transparency from NHS organisations after data breaches were uncovered further compounded the heartache, they added.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Deeply concerning’: NHS in England reports more than 3,000 incidents of staff snooping on patients’ records

items.title: Pill that mimics Viagra can slow Alzheimer’s progression, study suggests
items.summary:
Experts call trial results of medication that slowed cognitive decline by almost a third ‘very promising’

A pill that mimics Viagra by relaxing blood vessels and increasing blood flow to the brain can slow cognitive decline in people with Alzheimer’s disease by almost a third, a global study suggests.

Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, a condition that is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050. There is currently no cure.

Continue reading...
items.t: Pill that mimics Viagra can slow Alzheimer’s progression, study suggests

items.title: Drinking beer and spirits raises risk of acute kidney damage, study suggests
items.summary:
Research also shows consuming wine could cut risk, reopening debate on whether beverage has health benefits

Drinking beer and spirits increases the risk of serious kidney damage, whereas consuming wine offers protection against it, a study suggests.

People who drink nine units of spirits a week are 26% more likely to suffer acute kidney injury than those who consume only one unit a week.

Continue reading...
items.t: Drinking beer and spirits raises risk of acute kidney damage, study suggests

items.title: Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment
items.summary: Scientists have developed a new technique that uses magnetic nanoparticles to stimulate deep brain regions, dramatically improving Parkinson’s-like movement problems in mice without permanently implanted electrodes. The breakthrough could pave the way for less invasive treatments using injectable particles and wearable magnetic headbands.
items.t: Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

items.title: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.
items.summary: Scientists discovered that although people with and without autism show surprisingly similar average brain activity, individuals with autism exhibit much greater differences from one another, especially in regions involved in social understanding. The findings suggest that traditional research methods may be overlooking crucial differences that could help unlock more personalized autism support.
items.t: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

items.title: News Wrap: U.S. no longer considered a measles-free nation
items.summary: In our news wrap Tuesday, international health officials say the United States is no longer considered a measles-free nation, a Harvard study shows cellphone bans in some schools are leading to modest improvements in academic growth among students and maritime monitors say a gas tanker went up in flames in the Strait of Hormuz after it was hit by multiple projectiles.
items.t: News Wrap: U.S. no longer considered a measles-free nation

items.title: Why obesity affects men and women differently may be hiding in their fat
items.summary: Scientists at the University of California, Riverside have uncovered a surprising reason why males and females may respond differently to obesity. In a study involving mice, researchers discovered that immune cells traditionally associated with allergies and asthma can either protect against obesity-related inflammation or contribute to harmful metabolic changes, depending on their type and biological sex.
items.t: Why obesity affects men and women differently may be hiding in their fat

items.title: Doctors are raising concerns about U.S. babies born with measles
items.summary: Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb and can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns.
items.t: Doctors are raising concerns about U.S. babies born with measles

items.title: Public health expert reacts to latest measles milestone
items.summary: NPR's Scott Detrow talks with Dr. Ashish Jha, senior fellow at Harvard's Belfer Center and former White House coronavirus czar, about the news that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status.
items.t: Public health expert reacts to latest measles milestone

items.title: US loses measles elimination status amid worst outbreak since 1991
items.summary:
Infectious disease is now continually spreading after being eliminated for 26 years, with more than 5,400 US cases

The US has lost its measles elimination status, global health authorities announced, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.

The announcement comes as the US endures the worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths in 2026.

Continue reading...
items.t: US loses measles elimination status amid worst outbreak since 1991

items.title: U.S. officially loses its measles elimination status
items.summary: The Pan American Health Organization announced that measles is no longer considered eliminated in the U.S. It's classified as endemic now because a strain has lingered in the U.S. for over a year.
items.t: U.S. officially loses its measles elimination status

items.summary: The demands of work and home, and the creep of digital life, can seem to demand more of our attention each day. In this episode of "Settle In," speaker and executive coach Jovian Zayne talks with Geoff Bennett about how individuals can find small moments of respite and joy, and her new book, "Soft Landings for Hard Days."

items.title: Sleep paralysis: when you’re awake, but can’t move – or even breathe | Letters
items.summary:
Readers recount their terrifying experiences of sleep paralysis in response to an article by Amy Fleming

I experienced sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations from childhood and into adulthood, with the episodes only waning in my 30s (Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis, 11 November). I never spoke about them to anyone.

I experienced hallucinations in the form of severe perspective distortion (oversized bed and rooms) and full hallucinations/dream states, auditory hallucinations (screaming and loud thumping) and, of course, paralysis. I didn’t know at what point I was asleep or if I had woken and could easily slip back into a hypnagogic state. I only became aware of this state as an adult, having been referred to a psychiatrist on an unrelated matter.

Continue reading...
items.t: Sleep paralysis: when you’re awake, but can’t move – or even breathe | Letters

items.title: U.S. and Mexico officially lose measles-elimination status
items.summary: The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread — largely among the unvaccinated — at the highest rate in more than 30 years.
items.t: U.S. and Mexico officially lose measles-elimination status

items.title: Menopause symptoms aren’t always taken seriously. These female lawmakers plan to change that
items.summary:
From Utah to Louisiana, US states are making menopause care more affordable and accessible for midlife women

Melissa Shusterman was desperate for help with her menopausal symptoms: body aches, lethargy and brain fog, which she described as feeling “not myself”. The Pennsylvania state representative saw a gynecologist, a physical therapist, a chiropractor and a urologist. One doctor gave her lubricant, even though she’d already explained to him that sex was not the problem. (“Have you seen my husband?” she quipped.)

“I am more than lubrication,” Shusterman said. “I am a dynamic, smart, hardworking woman who wants to continue to feel good, so I can join my contemporaries, get back to work, and change things.”

Continue reading...
items.t: Menopause symptoms aren’t always taken seriously. These female lawmakers plan to change that

items.title: Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain
items.summary: Blockbuster weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro may do more than help people shed pounds, with growing evidence suggesting they could also influence brain health. Although studies have linked GLP-1 medications to a lower risk of dementia, major trials found that semaglutide did not slow Alzheimer's disease. Scientists suspect these drugs may be more effective at preserving memory and thinking abilities in people with obesity or diabetes, especially before cognitive problems appear.
items.t: Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain

items.title: I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker
items.summary: Has your doctor asked whether they can use artificial intelligence to take notes during an exam? It's very popular, and here's how to think through the pros and the cons of the new technology.
items.t: I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker

items.title: More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?
items.summary:
Thanksgiving is just around the corner, just as millions of Americans are expected to travel for the holidays. Another thing that's upon us? Cold and flu season. 

(Image credit: Thibaut Durand)
items.t: More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?

items.title: Expert behind NHS children’s gender services review says she cannot back conversion practices ban
items.summary:
Hilary Cass says draft bill is having ‘chilling effect’ on healthcare professionals and could pose a risk to parents

The expert behind a major review into children’s gender services has said she can no longer support proposed legislation to ban conversion practices related to sexual orientation and transgender identity.

Hilary Cass, a paediatrician who now sits in the House of Lords, initially indicated her support when the conversion practices bill was announced in the summer. However, she has now said the proposed ban is having a “chilling effect” on healthcare professionals and could pose a risk to parents.

Continue reading...
items.t: Expert behind NHS children’s gender services review says she cannot back conversion practices ban

items.title: Health organization to announce that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status
items.summary: The Pan American Health Organization is expected to announce that measles is no longer eliminated in the U.S. Record cases, lower vaccination rates and uncontained outbreaks led to the resurgence.
items.t: Health organization to announce that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status

items.title: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide
items.summary: A massive study of more than 340,000 adults found that moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular death, while even light consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was linked to increased risk. Although heavy drinking was harmful regardless of beverage type, the findings suggest that the relationship between alcohol and health may be more complicated than previously thought.
items.t: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

items.title: Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts
items.summary: A massive study involving more than 415,000 Americans has uncovered a concerning connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts. Researchers found that adults with the disorder had 57% higher odds of experiencing suicidal thoughts, with women and younger adults facing particularly elevated risks.
items.t: Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

items.title: 'It's close to bulletproof,' doctor says of MMR vaccine as measles cases rise
items.summary: Global health authorities are expected to announce that the U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health milestone it achieved 26 years ago. This past year, the number of cases in the U.S. doubled, making it the worst year in three decades. That was the focus of the latest episode of Horizons with William Brangham.
items.t: 'It's close to bulletproof' doctor says of MMR vaccine as measles cases rise

items.title: Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029
items.summary:
DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it

Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.

Continue reading...
items.t: Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029

items.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
items.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.
items.t: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder

items.title: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.
items.t: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought

items.title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
items.summary: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.
items.t: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain

items.title: A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that when and how often older adults nap could reveal hidden warning signs about their health. Researchers followed 1,338 people for up to 19 years and discovered that longer, more frequent naps were linked to higher mortality, while morning nappers faced a 30% greater risk of death than afternoon nappers. Each additional hour of daytime sleep was associated with a 13% increase in mortality risk.
items.t: A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death

items.title: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
items.summary: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.
items.t: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

items.title: Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss
items.summary: Sleep can have a powerful impact on weight. Research shows it can affect appetite. There is also a two-way relationship between sleep quality and diet.
items.t: Why sleep matters when it comes to weight gain and loss

items.title: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
items.summary: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.
items.t: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

items.title: What's the real cost of fast fashion? Ask the people making your jeans
items.summary:
Sydney Sweeney has great jeans, American Eagle Outfitters tells us. But who made them? And what are working conditions like in the garment factories of Pakistan and Bangladesh?

(Image credit: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg)
items.t: Sydney Sweeney has great jeans. Who made them? (Psst: Workers)

items.title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.
items.t: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

items.title: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.
items.t: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study

items.title: Laws limiting coal miners' exposure to toxic dust are in danger of being rolled back
items.summary: Coal miners who are exposed to silica dust are at a higher risk of black lung disease. Despite decades of advocacy, new efforts to regulate the toxic dust are under threat.
items.t: Laws limiting coal miners' exposure to toxic dust are in danger of being rolled back

items.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
items.summary: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.
items.t: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

items.title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
items.summary: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.
items.t: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss

items.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
items.t: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

items.title: The U.S. flu season is off to a very early start. It's hitting the South and West now
items.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Friday posted its latest update, reporting that seven states were reporting high flu activity last week, up from two states the week before.
items.t: The U.S. flu season is off to a very early start. It's hitting the South and West now

items.title: U.S. gives states another 6 months before they have to remove people from Medicaid for not working
items.summary: The administration clarified that while states still have the option to take action at the beginning of the year, they won't have to kick anyone off or deny coverage for failure to meet the requirement until July 1.
items.t: U.S. gives states another 6 months before they have to remove people from Medicaid for not working

items.title: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression
items.summary: A simple change to your daily routine could make a surprising difference in how you feel, both physically and mentally. University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regulate the body's internal clock, which influences mood, sleep, and overall health.
items.t: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

items.title: A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome
items.summary: Scientists have developed a promising new fiber supplement that improves gut health in people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) without worsening bloating, pain, or other digestive symptoms. The specially designed blend also improved gut-related anxiety and produced surprisingly rapid changes in gut bacteria, potentially offering a new way to manage IBS.
items.t: A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome

items.title: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms
items.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that hidden patterns of brain activity can predict Alzheimer’s risk years before memory problems appear, potentially offering an earlier warning than traditional biomarkers. The same patterns also reveal which brains are unusually resistant to aging, raising hopes for future treatments that could help protect memory.
items.t: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

items.title: Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis
items.summary: A new study suggests that the right kind of exercise could help protect young adults from early knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery. Researchers found that a four-month supervised rehabilitation program improved pain, muscle strength, and quality of life without damaging knee cartilage. The findings challenge fears that exercise worsens injured knees and could transform how patients recover from ACL reconstruction.
items.t: Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis

items.title: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't
items.summary: Yale researchers have discovered that certain prescription drugs, healthy diets, and exercise can measurably slow biological aging, while popular anti-aging supplements appear largely ineffective. Their analysis of 51 studies could transform how scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments, although whether these biological changes actually extend life remains uncertain.
items.t: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't
